effect: The result distinguishes checking identical wording from interpreting its later authorship and context.
reaction: The distinction is interesting, especially that identical words need not invite identical readings.

reason: This is the only available combination, and it can test how captions affect a copied image's interpretation.
expectation: I expect the identical photographs to support different readings through their captions, without the image alone settling whether attendance was voluntary.

effect: The final result shows that copies can serve opposing political accounts and that visible attendance alone does not establish consent. Both goals are complete.
reaction: The contrast between identical photographs and conflicting captions was a useful, concrete example.

mostWorthwhile.text: The crowd-photo comparison was most worthwhile: it connected reproduction and political framing to the practical limit of what an image can establish.

leastWorthwhile.text: The connection between the doubtful edition and Menard's identical words was initially less clear than the resulting distinction between wording and interpretation.

surprise.text: Identical words can invite a different reading because their imagined author and historical context change, even when their wording is settled.

arbitrary.text: The first pairing felt somewhat indirect: an edition showing textual doubts was used to introduce a case where the words match.

continue.text: Yes. The chapter's concise examples of checking authority and separating evidence from interpretation made me curious to see those ideas applied elsewhere.
